How I framed this (study note)

I recommend keeping the first release at feature parity with today's product and preserving the existing farm workflows, because MSD's stated priority for this project is time-to-market. Changing the user-facing behaviour now would add scope and risk without serving that goal.

In parallel, software starts on the ADLINK evaluation kit while Hardware assesses which parts of the existing carrier and enclosure can be reused, so the two tracks do not wait on each other. Feature parity is my scope recommendation; time-to-market is MSD's stated priority.

Reasoning and evidence

Supply continuity. If a gateway fails on a farm several years after installation, MSD still has to supply a replacement, so long-term module availability is an operational concern, not just a procurement detail. ADLINK publishes a 15-year product lifecycle for the new module. Before committing, I would ask Procurement to verify availability, lead times and lifecycle dates for our exact module configuration.

Local processing capacity. While the internet is disconnected, the gateway keeps receiving sensor events, writing them to the local database and serving a farmer who opens the web app. Those workloads compete for CPU and memory. To validate the benefit I would replay the same workload on both generations and measure throughput, missing events and web response time. Larger herds are a growth scenario; current numbers are unknown.

Security and maintenance. Secure boot means the device can verify that the software it starts is trusted. Moving to a maintained Linux BSP is a separate lifecycle decision: I would confirm with ADLINK which BSP release it supports, who provides security fixes, and for how long. Hardware support for secure boot and ongoing Linux maintenance are separate considerations.

AI capabilities. The i.MX95 includes a dedicated neural processing unit that could accelerate future models analysing the farm's sensor and tag data on the device, without sending it to the cloud. I would treat this as a growth capability, not a first-release commitment: I'd benchmark a candidate sensor-data model on the CPU and NPU to see whether the NPU reduces processing time or frees up CPU capacity before sizing any AI work.

If the current system already works offline, what does the upgrade buy us? Offline operation is already a requirement the current product meets, so the upgrade does not add it. The gain is capacity to process more data locally while preserving the farmer's experience.

Minimum change to run today's product on i.MX95

I weighed four approaches against MSD's time-to-market priority. My choice: upgrade within the SMARC family to the i.MX95, preserving the product's interfaces and farm behaviour and changing only what the new module requires. At M1 Hardware decides what can be reused and what must change. Scope: MSD brief
Option A Defers risk

Keep LEC-iMX6

No project now, but supply, capacity and security stay unaddressed.

Option B Chosen

Upgrade to LEC-iMX95

Stay in the SMARC family and aim to preserve the enclosure and interfaces; Hardware confirms at M1 what can be reused and what must change.

Option C More rework

Different vendor module

New supplier qualification and BSP for little gain over staying in SMARC.

Option D Highest risk

Full custom redesign

Maximum optimization but the longest schedule, against the time-to-market priority.

Chosen approach, R&D delta
  • Verify carrier compatibility and redesign only the affected circuits
  • BSP / Yocto bring-up and migration of the drivers this product actually uses (Ethernet, storage, USB and the sensor interfaces)
  • Port the app stack to A55 / 64-bit and validate offline mode
  • Verify power and thermal margins in the target enclosure
  • Verify IP67 early on a representative enclosure assembly
Chosen approach, NPI delta
  • EVT, DVT, PVT builds on the carrier once the M1 changes are agreed
  • Engineering and Compliance agree the EMC, safety and IP67 retest scope after reviewing the changes
  • Update production test fixtures and eMMC flashing
  • BOM and supplier setup for the i.MX95 module and pilot build
Acceptance: with the internet disconnected, replay the same sensor events on the new unit and compare its stored records and user-visible results against both the existing device and a known expected outcome. A short reconnection check then confirms that when the internet returns, the gateway resumes communication with the cloud exactly as the current generation does. IP67, offline: MSD brief
Why I scope it this way

Verify, then redesign. Committing to a full carrier re-spin before checking pin mapping, power and thermal compatibility risks redesigning circuits that did not need to change. I size the carrier work only after the compatibility review, so the schedule reflects the real change set rather than a worst case.

Why compare against two references. Comparing the new unit only to the existing device can hide a fault that both share. Comparing it to a known expected outcome as well catches a defect that is common to both generations, so the offline replay proves correctness, not just that the two behave the same.

Field replacement is an M0 decision. The replay proves the new server processes and displays events correctly, but it does not settle whether a new unit also has to replace a server already running on a farm with accumulated data. We decide this at M0. At M6, the device must meet the agreed event ingestion rate and web app response time. If field replacement is in scope, also verify backup and restore of the database history and farm settings.

IP67, verified early. Already at M1, Mechanical and QA check whether the seals, connectors, openings or the way the lid closes have changed. The aim is to verify sealing by M2, or earlier if a representative enclosure assembly is available, and this runs in parallel with carrier and software development.

How the IP67 decision is made. If the mechanical configuration is covered by previous-generation evidence, QA and Compliance record the basis for the decision. If a relevant part changed, we run the appropriate tests on a representative assembly. A water test alone covers only part of the IP67 requirement, which also includes dust; if the early sample covers only part of it, we state what was verified and what stays open for DVT.

Appendix: options compared (time, compatibility, risk)
OptionRough timeCompatibility and reuseKey risks
A, Keep LEC-iMX6No project nowFull reuse, no changeSupply, capacity and security stay unaddressed; a later migration may be forced and rushed.
B, Upgrade to LEC-iMX95Chosen~10 months (my estimate)Same SMARC form factor. Carrier and enclosure reuse assessed at M1. Early IP67 evidence reviewed by M2.Assumes enclosure reuse and at most one carrier design cycle; a second carrier spin adds ~6 to 8 weeks (my estimate).
C, Different vendor module~12 to 15 months (my estimate)Medium: new module, carrier rework, new supplierNew supplier qualification and BSP relationship; more integration risk for little gain over B.
D, Full custom redesign~18+ months (my estimate)Low: new carrier, possibly a new enclosureLongest schedule, highest technical and compliance risk and cost; conflicts with time-to-market.

What extends the other options. The 12 to 15 months for a different vendor module and the 18 or more months for a full custom redesign come from work that upgrading within SMARC avoids: qualifying a new supplier and its BSP, a larger carrier redesign, and in the custom case a new board and possibly a new enclosure with a full compliance and IP67 cycle. These are rough planning figures. The practical decision I am highlighting is the narrower one, reuse the existing carrier or adapt it to the findings from M1, rather than whether to leave the SMARC family at all.

My planning estimateThe M10 target assumes enclosure reuse and at most one carrier design cycle. A second carrier spin would add roughly 6 to 8 weeks. If the enclosure must change, the schedule updates with the scope of that change.
How I would validate the 10-month assumption

Activities leading to M4.5. Carrier design, prototype build and BSP bring-up all run between M1 and M4.5 on the hardware track, in parallel with software on the evaluation kit. They are the work behind the first offline event, not separate milestones.

How the four tracks overlap. Hardware runs the compatibility review from kickoff to M1, then carrier design and the prototype up to M4.5, then EVT fixes and DVT preparation, with a further carrier spin only if the EVT findings require it, which would add roughly 6 to 8 weeks. Software brings the app stack up on the evaluation kit from M0, runs offline tests there, and after the first integration at M4.5 continues testing on the EVT prototype. Integration and QA are not left to the end: the test plan and retest scope are set at M1, the first bench integration is at M4.5, and DVT follows. NPI starts at M1 too, with supplier and BOM setup, then fixtures, eMMC flashing and assembly preparation, so the line is pilot-ready at M8.5 without waiting for DVT to finish. The swim-lane chart on the slide shows each of these segments against the milestones.

Who validates it. Hardware owns the carrier compatibility review; Mechanical and QA own the early IP67 check; Engineering and Compliance own the EMC, safety and IP67 retest scope; Procurement owns the module lifecycle and lead-time check. The planning number stays mine as a target, not a commitment.

When. At M1 we agree the hardware changes and initial retest scope. By M2 we review early IP67 evidence and record any gaps. At DVT we confirm coverage of the final configuration.

What triggers a schedule revision. A needed second carrier design cycle adds roughly 6 to 8 weeks. If the enclosure must change, the schedule updates with the scope of that change.

Release gate. The M10 release is not a date, it is a decision. QA and Operations hold a Go/No-Go for the exact configuration that can be sold, and they sign it off against named inputs: the DVT results, the relevant compliance approvals, the PVT results, the released BOM and the approved software version. If any input is open, the item either closes before release or the release scope is narrowed to what is actually approved.
